utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Especially after three days I could have wished you a good morning. Could you escort Mr. Kirudja into the courtroom, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja. Please be seated. May I remind you, just as I did last Friday, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the usher could assist me in moving the ELMO just a little bit further. Thank you. Now I can see Mr. Kirudja. Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we left your testimony on Friday, we had examined Prosecutor's Exhibit 141 and a letter from Radomir Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, directed to you, informing you that there were another 1.233 people who wished to leave the municipality. I'd like to turn to the next exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 142, which is dated three days later. Mr. Kirudja, if you would inspect that briefly. This exhibit has -- is in two parts. It has a cover sheet bearing your signature and then a memorandum from Paolo Raffone. Do you recognise those documents, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you had been receiving information about what was transpiring in Bosnia, and let me turn to the second part of this exhibit, a memorandum from Mr. Raffone dated the 8th of July, 1992, the subject of which is "Arriving refugees from Bosanski Novi." Let me read this exhibit into the record. "On 7 July 1992, a group of 18 persons arrived in Sector North from Bosanski Novi asking for protection and assistance to cross the CFL toward Zagreb and other foreign countries. The civil affairs officer interviewed the group and arranged for the crossing on 8 July 1992. "The following information is based solely on the statements of these persons who have asked for anonymity for security reasons. In Bosanski Novi (BH), the Muslim ethnic group, 28 per cent, continue to suffer persecution, deportation, and intimidation from Serbian armed groups. The beginning of this crisis is traced back to the end of April 1992. The persons interviewed reported that all Muslims living in the town and in the neighbouring villages are ready to leave the area towards Croatia or other destinations in Europe. Previously, we reported the stadium in Bosanski Novi is one of the places where hundreds of persons have been held for screening following which they are expelled from the area toward unknown destinations." And there is a reference number to a previous report. "Reportedly all Muslims are forced to sign papers asking them to 'voluntarily leave' under the following conditions: Leave behind all personal property (including cars, personal effects, et cetera), swear that they were permanently leaving the area and that they will never go back to their houses. Following compliance with these conditions, they are issued a declaration from the local TDF commander in the milicija (or the mayor) allowing them to leave their opstina of residence. They are generally forced to leave in the direction of Dvor. It is reported that the local authorities in Dvor does not seem surprised at the arrival of the forcefully reported --" removed, I'm sorry -- "removed persons. They even show a cooperative effort to facilitate their way towards Croatian-controlled territories. "A calculated strategy to 'cleanse' the area of Muslims appears to have intensified beginning in May 1992. House burnings, deportations, summary executions, shooting in the houses, et cetera, are part of the present situation in the towns and villages along the north side of the BH border (Bosanski Novi, Bosanski Kostajnica, and Bosanska Dubica). Reportedly the milicija does not seem to intervene. Some mayors and other Serbs working in the opstinas have also been reported as trying to help the Muslims to leave their houses safely. In Bosanski Novi, the military police is reported to have its HQ in Hotel Una. There are reports of brutal torture in this hotel. "The persons interviewed believe that the political leaders know what is happening. Some of them attest to allegations that some high-level politicians in the SDS party are known to have given orders for actions against Muslims. Some of the refugees tell of a retaliatory policy of 'one Serbian killed on the front line, one Muslim man will be killed.' All of the men interviewed had been held for some days in the stadium of Bosanski Novi before being expelled. They report that every day some 30 new detainees arrive in the stadium. When the stadium is full, the guards take some of them away to unknown destinations. Some witnesses report that in the first 15 days of May, some 200 persons taken out of the stadium were shot dead nearby. Based on these interviews, the persons estimated that some 5.000 persons may try to cross the bridge between Bosanski Novi and Dvor in the coming days." And this letter is signed by Mr. Raffone, and it says it is released by Charles Kirudja, CAC. First of all, can you tell us what "released by Charles Kirudja" means, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, we are still mandated to deal with the Vance Plan in the UNPA, and every document that came up the reporting line has to be clear as to what it is that we are reporting, whether it is within our mandate or not. And when we were seized of this matter of refugees coming from that area of Northern Bosnia through Dvor to the sector, the evidence you have heard in the last few days has to be we are telling our headquarters that this matter is becoming a destabilising -- is becoming a destabilising factor inside the sector. So when these refugees, as this letter comes -- shows at the beginning, come into the sector seeking to cross, they are debriefed, and they are debriefed and that summary of what is happening is written out and brought to me by whoever I assigned. In this case, Mr. Raffone. When the issue is serious enough, then I did two things: I could have quite simply signed myself, because I have to decide whether it's a relevant issue or not, but in matters like this, I wanted to preserve the knowledge that the basic work was done by this officer and that the input into this was by the officer. The content, on the other hand, it's something that I worked with him to frame and to report within context, and therefore I had to sign the release of it. Otherwise, he might be questioned why he is spending the time outside the mandate area himself and suffer career implications by the bosses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did this information, Mr. Kirudja, give you additional insight into the organised nature of what was happening in Bosnia to the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, actually, it wasn't additional. It was now conclusive. It was giving us the last bits of necessary information for us to begin to make conclusions. And it has a few elements that I would like to draw Your Honours' attention to. As you will see, we are talking about 18 persons who are talking to us. We grant them anonymity so that they can tell us honestly what it is that they see, and now we start checking it out to see whether it corroborates information earlier received to us. And in the fourth paragraph of this memorandum, you will see that these 18 people are telling us elements that on Friday we looked at in the letter addressed to me by Mr. Pasic about what it is they were being asked to do. As you can see, leave behind all the -- leave behind all your property, swear never to return, but still being dressed up to look like voluntary, which explains the quotation mark, 'voluntary,' because by now it's abundantly clear there's nothing voluntary about this. You can see also the pressure building up on them. They want to go out of here. As the story unfolds, some of them are missing or feared dead, so by this time, if you turn the page, we are now saying there is a strategy to cleanse this place. So this memorandum, and my editing it, is to bring out this issue, and we are becoming now the exit point in the centre, in the UNPA where all these people are marshalled through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. If we turn to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 143. We will just spend a little -- a moment with this exhibit. This exhibit, Mr. Kirudja, bears your name and initials at the end. Do you recognise this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This exhibit is dated the same day as the memorandum on the previous exhibit, the 9th of July. It is -- the subject is "Assistance to refugees in the UNPA," and let me read the first paragraph to you, or for the record: "On 8 July 1992, Mr. Nogolica, chairman of the government of Croatia's office for UNPROFOR (Zagreb) conveyed to me the position of the government of Croatia regarding the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The refugees should be cared for in the place to which they have escaped within the UNPA and not be forwarded to Croatian-controlled territory where accommodation facilities for the refugees do not exist." Now, Mr. Kirudja, on the 9th of July, Croatia's position essentially was very clear: Don't send refugees from Bosnia to us. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact position is that if they come into your area where the UN is, that's where they will remain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Why did Croatia take that position?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now, the Croatians were engaged in a bigger issue, how to recover this area, the four sectors that are taken by the so-called local Serbs back into the sovereignty of Croatia toto. That was clear that was their major overarching interest and whatever we did there they wanted to make sure it was consistent with that issue. Point number 1. Point number two, this area itself where we were, the UNPA, had been evacuated, had been evacuated of its previous residents who were non-Serb. Their own intelligence knew that there was a continuation of displacement of people. Therefore, they took this position and told us clearly that we don't encourage this evacuation. If they come within the area where you are, we will not allow you to let them proceed further. It was clear they would rather not even have anyone coming in there, but that one, of course, is not something they can say because that area is within the mandate of the UN. So the most they can say what they said. They have to remain where you are. Up to that point. As you will see, that also changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If we turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 144, the next exhibit. Mr. Kirudja, if you'd just cast your eye on this document. This is a document dated the 12th of July, 1992, the author of which is Jens Brosted. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this document, in summary, describes two meetings which took place; one meeting that took place on the 7th of July and another meeting that took place on the 8th of July, and I'd like to start by drawing your attention to paragraph 8, which describes a meeting that took place on the 7th of July, 1992, and I will read this into the record. "On 7 July 1992, a meeting was held between the mayor, vice-mayor, and chairman of the Assembly of Dvor, a member of the staff for cooperation with UNPROFOR, vice-chairman of the Assembly of Bosanski Novi, as well as representatives of CIVPOL and DANCON. The problem of refugees from Bosanski Novi was brought up as something demanding a solution now if armed clashes were to be avoided. According to the Danish report on the meeting, the Bosanski Novi representative informed that the municipality had established two criteria for people who want to leave. One, they must sign a statement that they are leaving the area voluntarily (permanently); and two, they must certify that they have sold, exchanged, or donated their house and other immovable property to someone else. The Bosanski Novi informed that they had processed applications from 1.300 families who all fulfilled the criteria. They estimated that this amounts to a total of some 3 to 5.000 persons." Now, again the two criteria that are described by the Danish report that are required for a person to leave the municipality once again are the criteria that you had learned earlier; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had now become pervasively known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the 8th of July, there was another meeting, and in paragraph 3 of this memorandum, the participants of that meeting are identified as being the deputy mayor and the chief of the milicija as well as CIVPOL participants and a Major Rand from DANCON; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to paragraph 11 of this memorandum, this continues to relate to the meeting that took place on the 8th of July. In paragraph 11, let me read this: "The chief of police said that the refugee cases started some eight to ten days ago, but after the large increase it became a problem. Now many people already have exchanged their houses with Serbs from Croatia. The deputy mayor did not want to second-guess the reasons why people wanted to leave but later volunteered his own opinion. Some had been displaced in the politics of Izetbegovic. Further, after the fighting in the Cazin and Kladusa region and with the return of wounded and killed Serbs, Muslims in the area was getting afraid of revenge from relatives. As discussions got more frank, they did not contest that it was very questionable whether the request to leave had been signed voluntarily." Now, this is consistent with the conclusion that you had earlier reached; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, just for the sake of the transcript, I think it was a slip of the tongue where you said that people were displaced in the policy where it reads some had been disappointed in the politics of Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. Thank you for that correction. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the last part of this paragraph, there's -- the next sentence reads: "When I asked them to confirm that the mayors of Bosanski Novi and Banja Luka had been on the news in Banja Luka TV stating that Muslims and Serbs could no longer live together, they said it was not the mayor but the chief of the Crisis Committee in Banja Luka, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin." Now, this quotation that the Muslims and Serbs could no longer live together, had you heard that before, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on Friday I did mention that this is something we had heard all too often. And in this memo you're reading, please bear in mind it's Jens Brosted writing and he's hearing it too. It's not me writing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's hearing it on television.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's hearing it -- from the meeting he's hearing it secondhand reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he's hearing two things. If he was asked "What is going on here" -- he asked "What is going on here?" If it's a Serb speaking to him, usually he will hear, "We can't live together," and this is something that I mentioned is repeated over and over again, and he's demonstrating that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect do you think that kind of comment had on the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it had anything, because I'm talking about a common -- you mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effects, on the television. If you're able to give us that information.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're not able.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is a reported speech about what we had just been told in a room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then if we could turn to the next exhibit, Mr. Kirudja. This is going to be Exhibit 145. We'll be very quick with this exhibit. We've seen in the previous exhibits today reference to more people possibly coming across, wanting to come across into UNPA and transit through to Croatia. This memo, your memo is dated the 13th of July, and attached to it is a memo from Mr. Raffone. Do you recognise both of these documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the understanding that only my name and authority is being used. This particular one became a routine since my signature itself doesn't appear in front or inside. So it is a routine communication under my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the subject of Mr. Raffone's memorandum is "20 busloads of refugees from Bosanski Novi crossing the border towards Croatian-controlled territory through Sector North." And I'll read this very brief memorandum from Mr. Raffone, read portions of it. "Today an advance group of people from Bosanski Novi arrived at the gate of DANCON in Dvor and announced that on Wednesday, 15 July, at 1200 noon, 20 busloads of refugees will arrive in Dvor. The people have been advised that UNPROFOR will not be in a position to assist them in crossing and that the government of Croatia has given instructions to its border police not to accept their entry into Croatian-controlled territory." Now, this again is a reflection of Croatia's policy and -- which we will come across again in a few minutes, but now you have information that a significant number of people may be coming your way; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rehash. It's not even new. That's why it had become routine where the officer would feel comfortable to report just under my name. It's not new. This is 13 July. This figure of 5.000 goes back to 26th of May. So by now this matter had begun to be so preponderous [sic] and my officers had begun to understand it very well. The -- not only the policy of Croatia but all the elements of this. So by -- on this date, this matter is a continuing matter and it's not new, the numbers are not new, it's just a build-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we take a look at the next exhibit, OTP 146, also dated the 13th of July. And this exhibit is introduced merely to supplement the previous exhibit, Mr. Kirudja, which deals with the 5.000 Muslim refugees from Bosanski Novi, the information that you had been receiving. Do you recognise these three documents that are --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- make part of OTP 146?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These also deal with the imminent potential arrival of 5.000 displaced Muslims from Bosanski Novi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only to send it to another destination. It's addressed to ICRC. So we are trying to complete the information we are giving to -- the previous memo went to our headquarters, this goes to ICRC. Subject bears -- it's about the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document 147, Your Honour, relates to paragraphs 122 to 126 in Mr. Kirudja's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cast your eye, Mr. Kirudja, on 147, if you would for just a moment, and then we'll deal with the contents of it. Do you recognise Prosecutor's Exhibit 147, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these exhibits we jump ahead approximately a week; Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me -- and these documents represent -- one of these documents is quite significant because it represents a change in the policy of Croatia, and I'm referring to the letter from Franjo Greguric who was the Prime Minister of Croatia. It's the last page of the exhibit. Now, let me read this document into the record and I'll invite your comments, Mr. Kirudja. This is a document from the government of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Greguric, Prime Minister, it is dated the 20th of July, 1992, and it is addressed to Jose Maria Mendiluce, who was the special envoy of the High Commissioner for UNHCR in Zagreb. I'll only read a part of this exhibit. "Dear Sir: We received your letter describing the present situation of 'ethnic cleansing' in Bosanski Novi as reported by your group of senior officials from UNHCR Zagreb mission who visited the affected area. As you are aware, the Republic of Croatia did much more than our capacities have allowed us in providing care for 407.500 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina temporarily accommodated in the Republic of Croatia. The Croatian government, on an emergency basis, will, as a last solution, allow this group of 4.000 refugees, Muslim citizens of Bosanski Novi, to enter Croatia." Now, this letter from Mr. Greguric represents a reversal of position of the Republic of Croatia, does it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently a reversal but also evidently a reluctant and temporary emergency one. We are not reading it as a total reversal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What caused the changes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this time, this matter had become constant and troubling of everybody that was involved. As Mr. Greguric is saying to Mr. Mendiluce, he had received a letter from some of Mr. Mendiluce's staff that had advised him of, to my best understanding, by then the danger had increased for those who were in those areas of Serb-controlled area or in football field or somewhere in between trying to get out. So at this moment, he seemed to have been persuaded that these people were in mortal danger, enough to allow passage and a temporary reversal of the previous policy that they should not transition through the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to read part of your written evidence, paragraph 123.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document in front of me, my own testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Kirudja could be provided with Exhibit 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to be referring to paragraph 123, Mr. Kirudja, and I will quote this paragraph: "Having obtained the acquiescence of the Croatian authorities to accept the Bosnian refugees, we now turn to the logistical problem of evacuating and transporting these people. While I remain opposed to the transfer of these persons from Bosnia, viewing it as complicity in an ethnic cleansing that was surely going to recur, my views became moot once the Croatian authorities accepted the movement of the refugees and UNHCR agreed to organise the transit with UNPROFOR's assistance. It was clear to me that if we agreed to move these Muslims from Serbian-controlled areas of Bosnia, the Bosnian Serb authorities would simply consider it the 'first round' and we would soon be asking that we evacuate non-Serbs from the territory to the point at which it was fully 'cleansed.'" Why was it, Mr. Kirudja, that you believed this would encourage the authorities in Bosnia to continue to ethnically cleanse?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, by this time the number 4.000, as you have heard the testimony here beginning on 29th of May, numbers were much larger than 4.000. When the mayor came to see us in the -- first Mayor Pasic the first time, the numbers he was talking about from Bosanski Novi alone, say from the village of Blagaj, was 13.000. By the time that this information begun to filter from refugees themselves, from the telephone call you heard received in my office from the Mayor Kupresanin, he had already telegraphed that 15.000 were on their way from the areas that he named in that telephone. I'm talking about him mentioning areas from Bosanska Krupa, coming all the way through Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Kljuc, and saying 15.000 were coming and 15.000 more may also be on their way. By now these numbers had begun to be such that to be told that 4.000 is being allowed, obviously to anyone looking at it, you knew that is not where it's going to stop, and that's why my surmising that if you allow the first 4.000, it won't be the first time, it wouldn't the last -- rather, it wouldn't be the last time, it would just be a beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 148 as the next exhibit. Mr. Kirudja, these -- both of these documents that are part of the exhibit are dated the 22nd of July. Do you recognise both of those documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read from your memorandum dated the 22nd of July, just a portion of it, referring to -- I'm going to read portions BB and CC. The subject of this memorandum is "Transit of Bosanski Novi refugees through Sector North," and BB: "Sector commander given a plan involving the transit of up to 4.000 persons. UNHCR has requested DanBat to provide fuel for up to 55 buses and 200 cars as well as two ambulances and a rescue/tow vehicle." CC: "UNHCR recommends that UNPROFOR not be seen to be associated with the evacuation of Muslims and other minorities through the UNPA. During negotiations with local authorities which lasted four days (18/21 July), UNHCR has repeatedly denounced the policy of expulsion based on ethnic/religious 'cleansing' and intends to continue to denounce that policy." Now, Mr. Kirudja, did the transit through Sector North of people take place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, instead of 4.000 people transiting through Sector North, how many people do you estimate transited through Sector North once this permission had been granted?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to a rough estimate of more than 9.000. This thing was an all day -- more than all day. We started early in the morning, before 8.00. We were at the crossing point at Turanj way after 10.00 at night. So our rough estimate was more than 9.000 crossed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us just a few minutes ago that you anticipated that this would be the first of many requests. Let me turn to your written evidence at paragraph 128 of your written evidence, which I will read into the record: "On 8 August, I met with UNHCR special envoy Mr. Jose Maria Mendiluce to discuss the approach to be taken toward a new wave of refugees wishing to transit through Sector North. At the time, a report of the UN CIVPOL in Dvor estimated that the number of persons wishing to transit through the sector would amount to 8.000 refugees. Within a few days, that estimate rose to 28.000. It was clear to us that the UN could not repeat an evacuation similar to the one that took place earlier, let alone a new one of that size. To do so would be to participate directly in the reprehensible process of 'ethnic cleansing' unleashed by the Serbs in Bosnia. The UNHCR took the position that it would not succumb to any 'blackmail'. That was a response to the Serbian authorities claim that the UN had to assist in the evacuation 'or the Muslims will suffer.'" Now, what is the blackmail? Can you expand on what the blackmail reference is in your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the Croatian authorities relented and allowed the first evacuation to happen, it was because these refugees or displaced people were threatened with harm. We kept on hearing either indirect or overt or covert threats: If you don't assist, they will suffer, or it will be your responsibility, or we don't really require your assistance, we can solve this problem very easily. Words to that effect. And we felt that was pressure, hence blackmail, to allow a repeat. Pressure coming from those who wanted them to transit through the sector so that we can assist them move that many number of people, and that's what I characterised in this testimony as a sort of blackmail to let it happen again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who is making these threats? Were these people in official positions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now, a number of things had become routinely understood. You heard it repeated from one Crisis Committee to the other. These people are "voluntarily leaving," but they must sell their property, they must -- this routine, "We can't live together." So whoever is speaking, whether they are speaking for a small municipality or a large one, that pattern was heard over and over again. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your written evidence in paragraph 130, I will just summarise it. It appeared later that the request to evacuate 28.000 refugees seemed to be dropped, but now if I turn my attention to the next paragraph of your evidence, it reads as follows: "The Bosnian Serbs nevertheless came back to us, asking that we evacuate another 5.000 non-Serbs from the area. On that same day, a meeting took place in which this issue was discussed. The following persons were present: Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Dvor; Mr. Deganovic, a representative of the Serbian Democratic Party (SDS) in Bosanska Kostajnica; Mr. Dorin, an SDS representative from Kostajnica; and Mr. Murid Saflic, a representative of the Muslims of Bosanska Kostajnica. Mr. Deganovic said that they had a list of over 5.000 people in the municipality of Bosanska Kostajnica that wished to leave that area. He claimed that, to date, killings had not taken place in the municipality but that people were afraid to move about freely. He claimed that after Muslims were evacuated from Bosanski Novi, the Muslims in Bosanska Kostajnica also decided to move out." Now, can you comment on this particular paragraph, Mr. Kirudja, in particular your views as to what was happening in this municipality of Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was the second time Mr. Pasic is coming to us, and if there's a lead paragraph, I believe this should have been in August 19th. It should have been. And he brought with him these two representatives of the Muslim community, Saflic and Deganovic. Bear in mind the distant -- Bosanski Novi, for which he is mayor, is a ways west of Bosanska Kostajnica where these representatives are coming from. I don't know if you have the map in your mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, let me interrupt you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. The statement identifies Mr. Deganovic as a representative of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, and Mr. Dorin a representative of the SDS as well, and you referred to Muslim representatives. There's Mr. Murid Saflic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another Muslim --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another Muslim representative or was there only one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. The only one that is noted there, and if I've only noted one, chances are there was one. I can't always be certain sure of the names of individuals. You're talking about 14 years now, so it is not -- the events themselves may be clearer. The names of individuals are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So at least the Muslim representative Saflic is from Bosanska Kostajnica, and this one, he's talking about, in this sentence, that there are 5.000 people who want to leave the municipality of Bosanska Kostajnica. And it's what I was referring to, since I know the place, Kostajnica is far west from Bosanski Novi in terms of relative geography. And we are in Tapusko now, we are talking about the meeting in Tapusko. Kostajnica, we have a presence there. This is where the DANCON meetings referred earlier took place. On Friday we talked about a meeting over there where the DANCON people are talking about executions in the street and people being killed. Now here is a Muslim representative from that general area saying killings had not taken place, but people are afraid to move around. He is basically not at liberty, surrounded in the environment he was, to say that what we already said ourselves to the Serbs in that meeting, ourselves being UNPROFOR, where a soldier, a military observer, will tell them, "We observed some execution in some of the street. There are people missing." We can say that. He can't say that. So we read that by trying to say we are under pressure to get 5.000 people from here too. That's what it really simply boils down to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me just clarify something in this statement. Mr. Deganovic, who was a representative of the SDS, according to this statement, it says he, Mr. Deganovic claimed that killings hadn't taken place, but I take it from your evidence that the Muslim representative confirmed what Mr. Deganovic had said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Your Honours' guidance, if I look at my diary I can straighten that out because I have everybody identified in the diary who said what. If you like, I can clarify that. If you don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm satisfied. The Court may have some additional questions or the Defence may have some questions to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next exhibit, please, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This exhibit, Your Honour, relates to -- Your Honours, relates to paragraphs 138 to 146 of Mr. Kirudja's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you recognise the documents that make up Prosecutor's Exhibit 149?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me refer to paragraph 138 of your written evidence because this now deals with another meeting that took place. This is on the 19th of August, and let me read paragraphs 138 and 139 into the record. "Indeed on 19 August, UNHCR and civil affairs received at Tapusko a delegation of nine representatives comprised of both Serbs and Muslims from Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, and Prijedor." Now, we'll just stop there. Those are all municipalities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll continue: "All those presents were from Bosnia and included the following: Vlado Vrkes, SDS president in Sanski Most; Dragan Majkic, police chief of Sanski Most; Mr. Besim Islamcevic, representative of Muslims and Croats willing to leave Sanski Most; and Mr. Esad Hasanovic, the Sanski Most based representative of Muslims and Croats willing to leave Bosanska Krupa. Representatives from Prijedor were also present, but I do not have their names. Also present were Hans Linshol and Lars Neilson, field representatives from UNHCR." Paragraph 139: "The delegation intended to convince the UN to change its policy against mass evacuations associated with 'ethnic cleansing' and to assist in the organisation of another convoy through Sector North that would serve to evacuate up to 11.000 mostly Muslim 'applicants' for evacuation from Sanski Most, 8.000 from Prijedor, and 600 from Bosanska Krupa. I was given a printed list detailing 7.782 names of those 'ready' to leave 'voluntarily.'" Now, what was your reaction to this particular meeting and in particular receiving a list of 70 -- 700 plus Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now I have almost become used to the relentless nature of this pursuit. I thought I had heard -- or most of the things I was hearing had become routine and expected, until this time when I was handed a printed list. On those days computers were printing on a spiral, and it was about this big printout, computer printout from this meeting. The names were enumerated by the computer from number 1, and I just fast forward to the bottom. That's how I could be certain it was 7.782, because they were sequentially named. And then there were certain other comments that I don't recall, because unfortunately it is the one document that I never know what happened to. It was always at the shelf in my -- behind my desk in my office, and for some reason I never saw it again. This one disappeared, but not from anybody else, from maybe when we moved out of there, closing the mission, nobody paid attention to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the president of the SDS from Sanski Most, Mr. Vrkes, also told you something about the circumstances that permitted the Muslims to leave his municipality, and I'm referring to paragraph 141 of your written evidence, and I will read part of that evidence. He also said, and you're quoting him: "'We offered all those people a declaration for their signature.' The declaration in question stated that the signatories were leaving the area voluntarily, that they had no wish to come back to the area, and that they were leaving their property to the authorities in the respective area from which they were leaving." Now, this was quite similar to the process of ethnic cleansing that you identified taking place in Bosanski Novi; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, that's what I meant in that most of what I was hearing was repetitive. It is the same thing. It's not just identical from Bosanski Novi. There was a representative from Bosanski Novi in that meeting too. So it was the same group of people repeating. Despite everything that we had in exchange with them, despite that they knew our position with it, they were relentless. So this time I took to just listening and taking notes, that's all, listening to what they were saying. These meetings were invariably very polite meetings, it's not a position. So I just listened to something I have heard before. If I have told them our position and they have heard it, so there is no need to repeat so you just hear it over and over again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you believe, Mr. Kirudja, that the approximately 11.000 Muslim applicants who were leaving from the municipalities of Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa and Prijedor were leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. They took turns. The representative of Sanski Most who was in the meeting, you can check the -- took the turn to tell me, in Sanski Most, it's 11.000. In Bosanska Krupa, it's 600, or some -- everybody spoke on their area, and say we have so many applicants, they have all made these declarations. It's all very fine and dandy. The systematic nature of this whole thing was now out of -- undoubtful. It was obvious everybody was kind of presenting on their part. If they're from Prijedor, they spoke on Prijedor. If they are from Sanski Most, they would speak on Sanski Most. But the majority, the one to report the greatest number was Sanski Most; 11.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe those people were leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By now there was no question about me not believing it. I just took notes. I already knew, this is a repeat. We had already exchanged, had already told them that. That's not really doubt at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 142 of your written evidence, Mr. Kirudja, it reads as follows: "The UNHCR representative read them UNHCR's policy stating specifically that the UNHCR would not assist with the removal of people but that it would, rather, assist people in the location of their present residence or abode." Mr. Kirudja, what was the reaction of Mr. Vrkes to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Equally politely they listened to the UNHCR person talk. This is a meeting where they made their point, and I had invited those two representatives of UNHCR so I myself would not be the one to repeat the policy. I wanted the custodians of that policy to speak to them once again directly and clearly. So one of those representatives spoke to them and mentioned exactly what you see there. But they also, as I mentioned on Friday, underlined the policy: We are not saying UNHCR will not help at all, but we only help on location. If you don't move these people farther, if there is no more attempt to displace these people, we will come in and help. UNHCR told them that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Vrkes's reaction to that offer of assistance to help the people in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Invariably that will be listened to and ignored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you mentioned -- we know from this meeting there were two Muslims who were present, Mr. Islamcevic and Mr. Hasanovic who were with this Serb delegation from these three municipalities in Bosnia. Can you describe their demeanour to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people we also wanted to hear from. The presence of where we were is also indicative of a factor in conditioning their attitude. They were in the company of their Serb counterparts in the municipalities where they came from. They sat there and listened to the Serbs tell us that all these numbers want to leave voluntarily and they must leave. When it was their turn to speak to us, they spoke very deferentially to their Serb counterpart, evidently not using any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provocative language, going out of their way to say we have been treated correctly. The word is "correctly." I never knew what "correctly" means, but at least the translators will say "We have been treated correctly." And we need to get out of here before this summer or winter comes, and all these people are ready, we have relatives in these parts of Europe, we are ready to leave. And they will say that in a kind of resigned manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the exhibit itself, which is Exhibit 149, I want to just read the last sentence in paragraph 12, that reads: "At the --" and this is a paragraph that deals with this particular meeting that you have been testifying about. "At the end of the meeting, the delegation left feeling that the UN was an obstacle to what one of them called 'a humanitarian gesture by the Serbs to Muslims reached through the democratic process.'" Can you expand on that sentence?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representation made to us was so to give us or convince us this is something being done very systematically. We -- hence the reference to a democratic process. These were not refugees, these were applicants. They sought to leave voluntarily. They had the option to sell their property or give it to the state or donate it. Those are words used. And we were very fair with everybody according to the state law about this matter. So it was presented as fairly routine, non-threatening process. But we had heard it all before. We had already engaged them. We were not going -- we were not making this conclusion outside their earshot. We had already discussed with them the counter-intuitive nature of what it was they were presenting to us, and we had told them that this is now an action we couldn't support. We had gone as far as sending written admonition to the mayor, but they ignored all of that and started all over again. And therefore, when they were told by UNHCR the only thing you can count on us to do is giving you assistance in situ where you are. So once they give their speech, the UNHCR gives its speech, it was clear nobody was going to move, so the implication that we are uncooperative, and they could see that. Hence the nature of that sentence, because by the time they left the meeting, it was clear that we're not doing that. We are not going to organise the transition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into September now with the next exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 150. Mr. Kirudja, this is a document dated the 5th of September, 1992, and it is -- bears your name and initials at the end. It is entitled "Special Sitrep, Addendum to No. 5." First of all, could you tell the Judges what is a sitrep and what is its purpose.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, many of the memorandums that you have been shown are titled Memorandum, directed either to the director to whom I reported to or to the heads of UNHCR or to the heads of other NGOs. These are, as you have seen on the evidence, subject driven and the situation driven for the attention of whoever it is they are directed. We wrote that within the day what we were seized of the matter. We were also required routinely to write what was requested as a situation report. That normally would be at the end of the week. At the end of the week, we would look at all the elements that we had been reporting to and do a little more concerted analytical evaluative report, and that was called a situation report or, in short, sitrep. And it also was important. Situation reports had wider distribution. The others are restricted. So the analysis of the subject covered in a situation report are less detailed but more evaluative. And on this day, on 5th September, I decided a special situation report was due because a lot of things had been said. A lot of discrete reports had been sent, and I wanted to collect them all to give the picture as we saw it, and hence a special sitrep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 1 of this special sitrep, in paragraph 2 it describes the border between Sector North and Bosnia and Herzegovina can be divided into two sections; one -- and you've touched upon this earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One was that part of the border that was truly an international border, and the other segment was the part that divided Bosnia, that was controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, and Sector North which was described by the Bosnians as Croatian Serbs which, in essence, meant that there was no border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to paragraph 9 of this document, the all -- entitled "The all Serbian border segment," in this special sitrep you wrote the following: "The second border segment separates two territories controlled by Serbs on both sides. It is within DanBat area of operation covering Dvor and Kostajnica opstinas. Behind this segment of the border are the five Bosnian opstinas of Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Banja Luka, and Bosanska Dubica within which the phenomenon of 'ethnic cleansing' has been noted." Now, going on to paragraph 10, starting with the second sentence: "A stream of individuals arrives daily at Dvor via Bosanski Novi from Prijedor and Sanski Most seeking refuge. UN CIVPOL estimates that between 30 and 50 such persons arrive per day across the border into Dvor." I'm sorry, I didn't read that properly. "UN CIVPOL estimates that between 30 and 50 such persons per day cross the border into Dvor. The trend during the last few weeks suggest an increase in the number of individuals that enter the sector seeking protection and assistance." Mr. Kirudja, those people who were continuing to come across the border were continuing to be debriefed, were they not, by the people who were operating in Sector North? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they reporting essentially the same sorts of elements that you had been hearing earlier?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much so. We were -- if you -- if you mean -- when you say 30 to 50, though they were predominantly Muslim, they were not always Muslims. So if we debriefed Bosnian Croats coming in, it's not quite the same story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people who, nevertheless, were non-Serbs, essentially all non-Serbs who were coming out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that the Serbs were not coming across, but the only ones who engaged us when they come across are non-Serbs. Serbs did cross. They didn't need us. The border wasn't a border for them, and occasionally they would come in and we would find a house that used to be empty is now occupied. So it doesn't mean only the Serbs but those who drew our attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So into September, then, there are additional reports of ethnic cleansing taking place in the municipalities that are identified in paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I say in September, you were receiving additional reports from the refugees who are coming into Sector North. They were reporting to you ethnic cleansing in the municipalities that you have identified in paragraph 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally if we can turn to Prosecution Exhibit 151, which takes us into the month of October. Mr. Kirudja, this is a document dated the 8th of October, 1992. In fact, both of these documents are dated that date. Do you recognise both of these documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This second document in the exhibit, subject: "Civil Affairs Sitrep No. 7," is there a difference between a special sitrep which we saw earlier and a civil affairs sitrep?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the regular one. This is at the end -- at the end of the week, where my weekend was, where you put out one sitrep that was covering all and sundry of what it is that occupied us for that week and wasn't intended to focus on any particular matter, it was intended to be all-inclusive, an overall picture. The special sitrep was intended about what was going on in that -- in those two segments of the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this particular sitrep that's Exhibit 151, let me turn to paragraph 12 and let me read paragraph 12 into record: "As noted by Lord Owen and Mr. Cyrus Vance during their visit to Banja Luka, the practice of 'ethnic cleansing' appears to continue unabated. Towards the end of July, the UNHCR announced that the UN would in no way participate or do anything that would seem to encourage the practice. Specifically, the UN would not participate in arranging mass relocation of refugees from their houses if the cause of their displacement is the result of ethnic cleansing. In the last two weeks, this position of principle appears to have been degraded by. (a) a stream of small groups of refugees entering the UNPA daily in numbers between 30 and 50. In Respect of UNHCR's other principle of non-refoulement, the numbers of refugees coming into the UNPA have slowly but steadily increased." First question: What is the principle of non-refoulement? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Non-refoulement. This one you'll have to take my guess or get a UNHCR person to give you authoritatively. My understanding at that time was that once you receive refugees, internationally you can't push them away again. In other words, refugees, simplified, should find refuge in the first place they come into. You shouldn't send them somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now we've come to October, we're talking -- or you are talking about a process of ethnic cleansing. You have been witness to events from April of 1992, when we started this testimony and your first meeting with Mr. Pasic, we're now in October of 1992. You have taken us through a significant number of exhibits dealing with contacts you had with various representatives of the SDS and other political leaders from various municipalities in Bosnia. From your view, Mr. Kirudja, did it appear to you that what was happening in Bosnia was organised and systematic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this time, and "by this time" I mean -- what's the date of this memo? Pretty much by August, September, it was no doubt in my mind this was systematically organised ethnic cleansing in our area affecting mostly but not exclusively non-Serbs, especially Muslims. That conclusion was inescapable by then for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no additional questions of Mr. Kirudja. I notice it's now almost 10.30. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this concludes your examination-in-chief, Mr. Harmon. Would the Defence be ready to start cross-examination after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we adjourn, may I first invite Mr. Usher to escort Mr. Kirudja out of the courtroom. Mr. Kirudja, after the break, which will be until five minutes 11.00, you will be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is -- Mr. Kirudja has just given his explanation of what the principle of non-refoulement would be. There would be no need to cross-examine Mr. Kirudja on that issue because it's a concept which is well embedded in legal theory and in legal texts, and consultations with the Chamber indicates to me that the perception and the definition of Mr. Kirudja would not be the perception of what the principle exactly means in the opinion of the Chamber, but since it's a legal concept, there's no need to further examine the witness on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't going to anyway, Your Honour, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know, but it's just to make clear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Your Honour's direction coincides with our thoughts on the Defence side anyway, so there's clearly no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you arrived in -- I'll just call it Yugoslavia, in April 1992, and then, as you've told the Trial Chamber, it was the 19th of April when you eventually found yourself in Sector North where you were to work then for several months; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had come at least fairly recently, I think, from an extended period of work in Afghanistan. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Yugoslavia, or when you -- well, it was how long before you arrived in Yugoslavia that you were notified that that was going to be your next assignment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean between Afghanistan and Yugoslavia? I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you told, "Mr. Kirudja, your next stop is Yugoslavia. Your next assignment is Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was crystallized around March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we take it that in common no doubt with many other people as well educated as you are that your -- your knowledge of Yugoslavia, the issues in Yugoslavia, the different component parts of Yugoslavia was relatively basic for an educated person?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a lot, I would say. Depending, of course, what is by "well educated," but I don't think I had a lot of knowledge of the former Yugoslavia beyond what the UN was engaged in in terms of the Resolution, enabling Resolution, preparations. Yes, that's I was familiar with, not far beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, for example, before you were notified of your assignment in Yugoslavia, could you summarise what would have been your understanding, say, of the situation in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wouldn't -- it wouldn't have been that specific. The situation as understood by us when we were preparing to go into the mission was pretty much what the Vance Plan and its background indicated. There had been a conflict in the former Yugoslavia in the specified areas that I testified earlier where we were going to be deployed, and this was essentially a conflict inside of Yugoslavia. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I testified, the assumption was that all was okay. We were going to place our headquarters in Sarajevo and be seen to be neutral between the two capitals, Zagreb and Belgrade. Not specific information about Bosnia and Herzegovina beyond the fact that it is no more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a specific example. When you -- as far as you can remember, when you were first notified that you were being assigned or sent to Yugoslavia, would you have ever heard of or registered that there was an entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina called Republika Srpska or Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that would have been something obscure, not known to me at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was, as no doubt it often is when you get sent to a new place, it would have been inevitably a rather steep learning curve for you to get into the situation when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good way of explaining it. It was a voyage of discovery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you say in your statement that at the time that you arrived in -- well, I suppose it's fair to say you arrived in Croatia, because I take it that your actual personal base when you were out there was in Croatia at all times, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The testimony, the long one, begins with my arrival on April 6 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. But once you got into Sector North --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for practical purposes your personal base was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My personal base was right inside that sector. See the headquarter is Tapusko. That is inside Croatia. Is that what you meant in the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Croatia, in that sense, you said in your statement, and of course I'm lifting it out of context for the purposes of this question, there was no apparent problem anywhere in Bosnia. That's a slightly sweeping statement, and I don't think anybody would disagree that in its simple terms it wasn't true, but the -- when you say there was no apparent problem anywhere in Bosnia, can you please explain why from your point of view there wasn't an apparent problem.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a very graphic way comparing where we were, the point you just located, meaning Tapusko, physically it had all the earmarks of recent fighting; blown-out houses, burned shell, blockages at every few kilometres while you travel. Not so with Bosnia. As a matter of fact, when I arrived in Sector North, the easiest road wasn't even in Croatia, the other side. No. We just went down into Bosnia and then entered the sector from Bosnia because it was the most smooth, the easiest drive, no checkpoints, no houses blown up, nothing. The normalcy of the area was self-evident. Again, compared with what I just said with all the recent evidence of fighting in where we were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a nutshell, the part of Croatia you were in was -- looked and felt like a war-ravaged country; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part of Bosnia that you're referring to looked and felt like a normal, stable country in which people were going about their lives?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That's how I -- what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you record in your statement that by early April 1992, the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised by many countries, including the European Union - and just to remind ourselves, that recognition by both the European Union and the United States came on the 6th of April, 1992, so that's just before you wound up in Sector North. And then you said "This precipitated the deterioration we began to witness in Bosnia, and it also impacted heavily on our work within Sector North." Now, my first question is this: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Stewart and Mr. President, if counsel could refer to the paragraph number when quoting Mr. Kirudja, it would be helpful to me, and it might also be helpful to Mr. Kirudja in referring to the particular being quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That is a simple piece of help to give. This is paragraph 14, 1-4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware in April 1992 of the enormous strength of feeling among Serbs about the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The effect of that strong feeling began to be evident much later, probably 1993. By then, we didn't connect that strength of feeling with the event itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you now know, with the benefit of hindsight and your greater experience of this region, that that strength of feeling certainly existed in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. By 1993, I knew its importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- and then in the next paragraph, which is numbered paragraph 15 of your statement, you say in the second sentence, it begins on the third line: "It later became apparent that the Serbs inside the UN protected areas aspired to be part of what became popularly known as a plan for a Greater Serbia, apparently inspired from or coordinated in Belgrade." Now, the first question is this: What you say "what became popularly known as a plan for a Greater Serbia," who are -- in your reference there, who are the populace or the population that you're talking about there among whom it became popularly known as a plan for a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to -- we were a community, obviously. When we were part of the UN, there was us, the international community, deployed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the midst of a war zone in the sector, and we were listening to what the residents or citizens or whatever you call them who lived there were telling us, and we heard things like, "We would like to live in our own country," as I recall one of the testimony, and I gave -- I'm puzzled when they tell me in the sector a mayor, a civilian, local civilian says to me, "We would want our -- to live in our own Serbian country." And I'm puzzled at that. I said, "You mean this sector?" "No, but our own country." It began to trickle from that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trickle in the sense of -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of explanation, of expansion of the meaning. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And you came to see, I say gradually, I'm not suggesting too slowly or anything, but you came to see what was meant by that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then -- so after you began to see what was meant by that, how would you summarise or describe that popularly known plan for a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I would describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, your paragraph 15 -- you have that in front of you, don't you? I think -- you've got your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I'm saying there is a sentence there describing how I began to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about where you go on to -- to the attitude towards the borders.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it wouldn't have been all that surprising at the time, do you agree, Mr. Kirudja, if the international border was regarded as quite porous, because after all, until extremely recently these had all been one country, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very well demonstrated. When I arrived it didn't matter where I started driving into Bihac. For the reasons I didn't go into, I had to frequently go into Bihac. There in the testimony the part of the -- this part of the testimony why we had to go to Bihac so frequently. The point I'm making is in response to you: There was no hindrance on 19th of May, the first few weeks of May, to drive into Bihac, into Velika Kladusa. The crossing points there were not manned. There were no soldiers. Indeed what you say, it was an easy border, yes. But within weeks, it separated into part of it, and here's the border, second part of it, not so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you get the feeling that the people that actually lived there and had lived there all their lives perhaps didn't immediately adjust and adapt and change their way of thinking and acting to fit the new international borders?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Counsellor, I don't understand the question. When you mean the people exactly, please be --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about the border being -- the international border being quite porous. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us. For us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for us crossing that border, at the beginning, we could go in and out with no restrictions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's one point.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I suggest to you it's clear that in the last sentence of paragraph 15 when you talk about the international border was quite porous and the Croatian authorities realised quite early that this was being used by the Croatian Serbs to re-populate the UNPAs with Serbs, you're clearly talking beyond --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So the international border was porous in the sense that it was porous as far as people were concerned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the point, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I also specified very soon, within weeks, part of it wasn't porous for non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about -- so the plan for a Greater Serbia, now, from the slightly more local perspective that you were adopting where you were, thinking of course of your area of responsibility, Sector North and the adjoining area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's one aspect. Did you have in your mind as you came to appreciate what the situation was that -- that this popularly known plan for a Greater Serbia had a more -- had a wider ambit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- in retrospect and much later, yes. And I got to see even the bigger dimensions we haven't spoken here about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was -- that bigger dimension, that was something, the way you're describing it, that perhaps quite naturally a dimension that you gathered over the longer period as you were working out in this region and began to piece things together in your own mind.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kirudja, I'm asked to ask you -- I'm always being asked to slow down myself, and I occasionally remember to do that. I'm asked to ask you, please, if you could just pause at the end of my question before you begin your answer, because that gives an opportunity to the interpreters to do their job.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsellor. I am always reminded of that, and I shall endeavour to do so. I realise I haven't quite done it immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you and I are members of the same club. We're each being reminded of these things and we're each struggling to remember. So we will agree to do our best, the two of us, on that. But you've implemented the instruction immediately, I note. The -- Mr. Kirudja, the -- you -- you talk about -- you use the phrase about this popular -- popularly known plan for a Greater Serbia, you say apparently inspired from or coordinated in Belgrade. Now, was that something that was -- the fact that it was inspired from or coordinated in Belgrade, was that something that was apparent to you in as early as the second half of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, the intent of that paragraph was kind of chronologically implying by that stage when the testimony was being taken from me, we were already in May. It was apparent but it wasn't certain. We were seeing reasons to think so, but we were beginning to learn what it was and how far. At the stage the paragraph is written, the date is around May. So apparently referred also to that time, to what we were seeing, and recognising we weren't concern of how much that coordination or inspiration there was. We were on a learning stage of that. Signs were there, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not attacking your phraseology here, Mr. Kirudja, just trying to get it clear. So it would be a fair summary, would it, to say that around this time in May you and your colleagues were really saying to yourselves, Well, I wonder exactly what's going on here and who is driving this and where all this is coming from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were wondering what the signs we were seeing meant, and they would point at there must be some coordination because, example: Various local authorities that we were dealing with when we arrived, somewhere in this testimony it's mentioned, tended to disappear from time to time, and the next thing we know is that they're in Belgrade, the local Serbs, officials. We also could see life had changed a lot, like currency, money. The local currency had disappeared, the dinar. But there was somebody paying the bills of the official activities, and the -- the bigger interaction we had at this moment by nature was military. I spent an awful amount of time dealing with the military, the Yugoslav National Army command. And the signs were there, especially in the military, of connection all the way there. What they meant, the extent to which we could say yes, it was being run or -- that's what I'm talking about. The signs were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else, then, that you can recall specifically at the time which pointed to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it began mostly with the military part, then with the civil authorities. And it wasn't unnatural, by the way. It was something also we needed to do. We had a liaison office in Belgrade because the signatories to the nation's authority were both Belgrade and Zagreb. So it wasn't actually unnatural. That was expected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the -- the next paragraph of your statement, that's paragraph 16, 1-6 -- well, before we go specifically to that question, just following up what you've just said. You've described to the Trial Chamber very clearly what your responsibilities were, you personally and the group - I call it that - of which you were a member. Would it be correct to say that although it was a very interesting question and one that you would have no doubt explored frequently in discussion with your colleagues, that actually working out where the inspiration or coordination was coming from was not actually part of your official functions or responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some respects, it was. If we were going to achieve the first priority of demilitarising, demobilising and disarming the military units, then it's part of our mandate, and the JNA was a previous official structure, therefore, coordination would be natural from the headquarters.
