However, if you notice that instead of going in the direction towards the mandate you are seeing a transformation of these military units in a direction contrary to what the mission says, then you don't want to imply there is an inspiration from the headquarters who signed the mission presence. So your question ends up having a yes component and a no component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So moving on, then, to paragraph 16, as I said I was about to, 1-6, a sentence -- and I think I should give you the context. About five lines down in your paragraph 16, you say that you reviewed the documents related to your work in Sector North. That's for the purpose of your evidence, your statement. And then you say: "My remarks follow the presentation and review of this documentation, deal with the following subjects," and then "Establishment of the UNPAs, JNA withdrawal from Croatia, UNPROFOR's relations with Republika Srpska Krajina, officials in Sector North, and to a lesser extent in Knin." And then you talk about RSK and Bosnian Serb collusion in the ethnic cleansing of Muslims and other non-Serbs in Northern Bosnia, which of course has been a central feature of your evidence in this case so far. "Bosnian Serb," it's -- of course it's a specific term in the sense of is a person from Bosnia and are they a Serb. That's the easy bit, if you like. But as a term, "Bosnian Serb," I wonder if you could be more precise to help the Trial Chamber as to who you are referring to when you talk about "RSK and Bosnian Serb collusion."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this testimony was being done in 1999, and the substance of what it covers was happening as far back as 1992. So there is a process of summarising it as well as recollecting. So that paragraph summarises for the people who were interviewing me the main elements of what I was going to talk to them about. So the language, counsel is correct, is broader and slightly brought to date in terms of time. When we were on the ground, when we started, RSK didn't exist, was not supposed to exist. It stands for Republic of Serbian Krajina. That's what eventually it became, because they used that term to describe -- to describe themselves by the end of the year or so. At the beginning, we were calling them what I testified earlier as either "local Serbs" or "Croatian Serbs" for the RSK abbreviated in this paragraph. On the Bosnian side, we had no even terminology at the very beginning refer to them other than residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina until I myself, in a meeting with Mr. Pasic, was given a term, and that was in May when I asked "Who are 'we,'" because you are in Dvor, part of Croatian Serbs, and you are talking to me about a cross-jurisdictional matter into Bosanski Novi, across an international border, and he gave me the term which he prefaced with "new reality" called Serbian -- Serbian Republic of BiH. So those terminologies were fluid and evolving, and my main testimony here was to try to capture them first and then go into details as the testimony opened up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So -- well, we could go on, then, perhaps at later points in your evidence. I think what you're saying is correct, that really you're just trying to give the chapter headings --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in paragraph 16. Overall -- I want to ask you about General Nikovic. Overall, at the conclusion of your dealings with him, what was your assessment of him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very positive one. As an officer of -- a military officer, General Spiro Nikovic impressed me as a person of integrity and a person basically doing their best to achieve the results his orders required. He was that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just looking at paragraph 27 of your statement, please. It's at the top of page 7. You report a specific exchange with General Nikovic, between you and him when you're asking about a number of people in Karlovac possibly being provided safe passage into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and General Nikovic replied, "Never. They say they're Muslims, but they're not. They're trained in Austria and Germany. We will prepare a concert for them if they try to come across." How would that particular -- how would you fit that particular exchange into the overall positive assessment of General Nikovic which you have just described?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, it's part of the reason I had a positive assessment. He didn't speak to me in code, he didn't speak to me -- he spoke very direct in a matter, and in this case he was kind of half jovial, half threatening, but he left it no doubt that this group of people gathered in the football field - now, this is a different football field, Your Honour. It's in Karlovac --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- not in Bosnia. It's in Karlovac. And there are people in ordinary cars who want to come back into Bosnia through the sector. Almost a reverse. They are not refugees, and they want to come in. And he looks at me and, "Go tell them we're going to prepare a good concert for them." And of course I said, "You're not going to play music." And he said, "No, they'll understand what I meant." So he was the kind of person who spoke directly. He left no doubt what he meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you contrast, if we go on to paragraph 30 and 31 of your statement, you contrast, first of all, what General Nikovic, you describe his attitude. You say about six or seven lines down in paragraph 30, do you see the sentence beginning "Specifically..."? It's about four lines from the bottom of paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. "Specifically, he --" and that's General Nikovic -- "seemed well-disposed to seeing that the UN mandate was implemented fairly and in full. And therefore, what UNPROFOR agrees with Belgrade will apply to Serbian Krajina." And then in paragraph 31, the very next sentence of your statement, you say: "As it turned out, however, the local Serbs had a different agenda. It later became clear to us that the local Serbs intended to consolidate their hold on the contested territory of Croatia." Can we take it that in both those sentences, both those references to local Serbs there mean the Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were the ones who, in your view, were appearing to seize on an apparent loophole in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to describe some of the -- this is still in paragraph 31. You go on to describe some of the broadly military aspects. You say about five lines down: "Thus the local Serbs..." so same local Serbs again, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Thus the local Serbs proceeded to set up their Territorial Defence forces right at the heels of the JNA's withdrawal, to transform their milicija into a heavily armed police force," and then you describe repainting of military vehicles, change of uniform to blue uniforms. And then you say, top of page 8: "In addition to the blue uniformed milicija (police) a parallel force still sporting the camouflage green colours of the former JNA also existed." And then you describe some of that parallel force and talk again about the local Serbs justifying the maintenance of these armed forces. At the time, first, did you know or have any good idea under whose control that parallel force was operating?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your knowledge or belief?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer I'm going to summarise, Your Honour, will be found later as you go on in this -- in summary, more or less, 34 and 35 where it is also detailed the names of the units. So I'm going to summarise counsellor's question. The sector where we were deployed -- actually, both Sector North and Sector South were part of the command structure before we arrived in the previous system that was known as the 10th Corps, the command headquarters in Bihac where General Spiro Nikovic had his headquarters, where we spent enormous time trying to get his plans to demobilise all these units. So those units, now limiting myself to Sector North, had three command structures. One was known as Kordun and was commanded by a colonel called Cedo Bulat. The second -- and Kordun covered a number of opstinas. I won't go into all the details. The second command structure was known as Banija, and it also covered a number of opstinas inclusive of Dvor, inclusive of Dvor and Kostajnica, and that was commanded by initially a general from Montenegro who didn't last for more than a few weeks, but later on for the longest period came under the command of a colonel known as Colonel Tarbuk. And toward the south of the sector, in the opstina of Slunj and Plaski, it was under a command known as Lika command, and that Lika command went down, had a headquarters in two places, some of it held at Korenica and some of it -- a remnant of it, because of the boundaries, was not covered by Korenica. So yes, I knew who the commanders were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you -- you say that you were informed by -- this is reference to paragraph 33 of your statement -- that you were informed by General Nikovic that the date for JNA withdrawal from the UNPAs had been set as the 25th of May, 1992. Did you know by whom that date had been set?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once we were ready to put in place that major element in the Vance Plan that required demobilisation, demilitarisation, and handing over of the weapons for storage, that couldn't be done sector by sector, it became obvious as we went into this. We would make our own negotiations for demobilisation and demilitarisation within the sector and send the sector commander, the military commander would send those plans up the chain all the way to General Satish Nambiar, the force commander. But so would other Serb commanders in Sector South, Sector West, and Sector East. And they were coordinated in the force commander's office, and the force commander's office had to coordinate it with the two capitals, Belgrade and Zagreb, and the date for simultaneous demilitarisation was set for May 25th, all sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about an incident that you describe at the end of April in paragraph 38 of your statement. You say: "I also note that the 30th of April was the first time we encountered people who had left Bosnia under duress," and then this is one family that you describe. And I just want to clarify with you. You say there was the father with a Turkish passport, the mother, a Yugoslav born in Splitska in Bosanski Novi, and a daughter. Can we take it the daughter was quite a small child, was she?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say all were residents in Switzerland. So can you just explain that? Where was -- do you remember, where was their base and where were they ultimately trying to get to and from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, this -- this was -- this would have been a totally Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. normal, non-interesting event in the course of a human day. This is a man who used to have a job in Neuchatel in Switzerland. His wife was back in Splitska, and they had driven their car -- by car for whatever reason, unknown to us, into Bosanski Novi, and they were trying to come out with their child and getting frightened and getting fearful for their security or indeed their lives. And that was what caught our attention in terms of abnormality, because when they came into the sector, the Serbs in the sector continued that treatment that made them fearful for their life. It was almost middle of the night, the chief -- the UN civil police called me, and because they were so scared we went to a Vojnica hotel and put a guard of UN police around what is a normal family, and then we began to talk to them and ask ourselves what's so difficult letting them pass through, and that's what's implied in that paragraph. That first sent our feelers up to try to understand something unusual is going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get it clear first of all. They were heading back to Switzerland, were they? That was the idea.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the father had perhaps come home from his work, had he, from Switzerland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may appear so. I'm not quite sure exactly, but they were trying to come out from Bosanski Novi to go back to Neuchatel where he was based or had work to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the way you've described it so far, their problems arose when they'd got into Sector North.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less continued, not arose. They seemed to have sensed danger as we talked to them. When they got into the sector, rather than face less danger, they seem to have felt more of the same, almost without quite understanding, us or the family, why it was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they'd left Bosnia under duress. Now, just to clarify, Mr. Kirudja, that -- this isn't a question, it's really just a supplement. It's a supplement to the question. Left Bosnia under duress clearly means that the duress had occurred in Bosnia before they got into Croatia, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got that distinct impression from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you -- you've said that they -- they were wanting -- in this case, they clearly were wanting to go back to Switzerland because that's where the father worked; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where -- just describe to the Trial Chamber where was the duress given that apparently they wanted to go back to Switzerland and they had been able to leave Bosnia. Where was the duress in -- that they'd experienced in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived in the sector, Counsellor, it was clear they couldn't leave that sector. The Serbs were trying to arrest them. I'm talking about the Serbs in the sector. In Vojnic, where they were in a hotel, they would have been put in gaol except for our intervention in that hotel by putting our own security people outside their door 24 hours, and me trying to ask them why can't she leave? The first thing they told me is that she and the husband can leave if they leave the car behind. And I said they need the car. They have travelled so far. And they would tell us, this has been occurring all the way. We've been trying to get to the next part, trying to nice the next official who wants to put us in gaol. And that was happening in Vojnic where they, too, wanted to arrest her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vojnic is in Sector North; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And all they wanted was to transition out with their belongings in the car and the car itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's the -- it's -- when you say it was evident that the Serb authorities not only didn't -- did not tolerate their presence but would also not guarantee the security, leaving aside the question of who exactly the Serb authorities were for the moment, those were the Serb authorities in that bit of Croatia, i.e., Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly for Sector North.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about the Serb authorities, were you sufficiently closely involved with this particular matter yourself to be able to be more specific as to who or which Serb authorities were -- you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular, yes. I met this couple personally, and I did get involved because from the very beginning to try to understand how -- I was the only one who could request the police to provide the security. They were our police, I mean civil police, to do what they did to keep them safe. I was also the only person who could go into Vojnic police station and demand to know why this couple couldn't leave and get out. So yes, I was directly involved in their problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you talk a little bit later on in your statement, it's really starting around paragraphs 41, 42, a passage of your evidence relating particularly to General Nikovic. He gets an extra letter in his name quite often, but it's -- in the statement it's the same person. In paragraph 43 of your statement, you describe -- I wouldn't go all through the previous paragraphs because that's your evidence. You say in paragraph 43: "The JNA has problems because some local units do not want to give up their weapons." And then you say you understood that to mean that there was resistance by local Krajina Serbs to his plans for eventual demobilisation and demilitarisation. And at this time we're just three weeks from the date that's been set, aren't we, for the JNA withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say, "The general went on to recount with some unmistakable relish the last battle between his JNA forces," and so on. And then you went on to say there were eight Croatian army brigades in Western Herzegovina and around Bosanski Brod and Derventa. "This statement was implicit explanation of why he and other local Serbs justified the needs for weapons that the JNA planned to leave behind." Now, I don't want to be too nit-picky, but when you talk about General Nikovic and local Serbs, are you putting General Nikovic in the category of a local Serb?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that point yes, because he commanded them. Remember I mentioned to you that the entire sector was his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But again here it looks as if when you talk about local Serbs as a category you are still here talking about the Croatian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inside. And Counsellor, I don't know the exact paragraph since you are picking them in the order of your interest --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant to say 43.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I meant the evidence that he himself was later on counted a non-Serb and left the sector is in the direction I think you're going. He left himself and he said here that he was counted among those who were not local Serbs and was relieved of his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as it happens, Mr. Kirudja, you are completely right about the direction in which I'm going. The -- so -- well, next page is the direction, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We go on to the question of General Nikovic's removal, his abrupt removal, as you describe it. It's the last few lines of paragraph 44. As commander of the withdrawing 10th Corps, and you interpreted it as manifestation of a policy revision somewhere in the hierarchy of Serbian military command. Now, first question is this: You talk about somewhere in the hierarchy of Serbian military command. Was it your clear impression that this decision abruptly to remove General Nikovic was taken somewhere within the military?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Counsellor, it is part of the earlier question you asked me when I spoke about inspiration and coordination from Belgrade, the extent of which I was trying to find out, and my response to you earlier was the biggest indicator was in the military first. And it was expected because of the situation that existed before. So here was a commander who was charged only weeks before with obtaining the demilitarisation and demobilisation of former JNA units according to a UN mandate. And he goes about it and gives a complete plan due to be implemented in two, three weeks' time. Then he is abruptly removed. That is a reference to if it was all normal, again common sense would say he'll go on until he completes his job, demobilises, when he's finished, he goes home. But three weeks before it's done he's abruptly removed. That's the reference. The only guess we could have answered is something has changed. And in this case, when you say was it all in the military command, it may or may not, because this is a lieutenant general. He only needed one more star to be at the top of the range. So once you are there, the distinction between all military and political is hard to do at that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you -- perhaps you can't add anything to what you already said, but can you add to how you read General Nikovic's removal, what it was about, what it was for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, not only was he removed abruptly, but one part of his previous command served me notice, and I recount that in brief here, go tell -- they said to me, "Go tell the General Nikovic if he ever sets foot here, we're going to arrest him." You can see the bizarre of that. If he's a three-star general and there is a colonel now, who is below him telling me not only has he been removed he's a persona non grata in this area. And I didn't take that lightly. I remember it was at night, and I decided to -- and I asked him, Do you want me to pass that message? He said, Yes, we know you talk to him. We want you to pass that message to him. So I drove about 8.00 at night into Bihac to try to tell him, if you come across this side, they're threatening they'll arrest you. So again it adds to my feeling that a lot has changed abruptly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The impression being conveyed, is this correct, Mr. Kirudja, is that you've indicated that you had a high regard for General Nikovic. Is it correct the impression that you're giving is that you actually had quite a warm personal regard for him as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the sense that up to that moment, he was doing correctly and forthrightly what we wanted -- what we were there to do. We asked for a demobilisation plan, he gives one. He gives the date. He gives all of that. What is there not to like? That's my job there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By contrast, Mr. Lazarevic was not your favourite person, as things emerged, was he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- only years -- I'm learning what probably was for me at that time I only began to feel he was an impediment. He was a destabilising factor, but I didn't know the full length. Only now, years later, I'm learning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you -- in the next -- well, and then you say General Nikovic appreciated the warning that you gave him. Can you say what happened to him then? First of all, immediately. Do you know what happened to General Nikovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only took a couple of days for him to hang up his boots, to use a military expression, meaning to take off your uniform and go home. And for a while he disappeared from my radar until in 1994 -- late in 1994, when I was in Belgrade in a different capacity, he showed up for a courtesy call in my office with a bottle of wine, and then he explained me he had returned to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you -- you go on in your statement, at paragraph 46, to describe an occasion on which you -- well, the particular problem you had with a Muslim interpreter, Indira Kulenovic. You describe that. And then you say, about six lines down in paragraph 46: "I went to the Vrgin Most police station --" I wondered whether Richard Branson had gotten into the territory, he's everywhere, that man, "... the police station and was presented with a list of charges against her, which included the following," and then you enter into Krajina with valid papers, being employed and so on, and then being a foreigner. You describe that, Mr. Kirudja. Just the question: Was it really as simple as that, the charges against her included being a foreigner?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Counsellor, it was the first hint to me -- what is the best way you can say. The non-sequiturial nature of the charge. Ms. Kulenovic is a resident of Tapusko. She is of Muslim descent but she was a resident of Tapusko and we had hired her as an ordinary, local interpreter. She now gets arrested by the chief of Vrgin Most, that is the police chief, and when I arrived later and towards the end of the day I go straight into the police station to be given the charge sheet, and in there there was the word "foreigner." You see, that attracted my attention because, coupled with a previous demand by Lazarevic conveyed to me by Mr. Lazarevic and others that we need to get permission from the Republic of Serbian Krajina before we can hire their citizens, and an attendant demand that we want also to check the passport of all your international people who are here in our Republic of Serbia Krajina. The term "foreigner" was therefore not a simple matter. It was part of the core charge, the result of which was, as explained here, when I gathered enough to know that she might not be so safe, it was easier for me to arrange for her transfer to Bihac where actually she was born and put her in our liaison office over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you, particularly arising out of this incident involving Ms. Kulenovic, you say in paragraph 47 that it was apparent to you that the local RSK officials were increasingly acting in unison. Is it fair to say to start with that you -- up to a point you would have wanted them to act in unison in the sense of having a unified approach in their dealings with your organisation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Counsellor. No. That was the problem. According to the mandate, the only authority recognised in each of the -- of the locations we were is the opstina, the municipality, and that meant the mayor and the chief of police. So the only person with authority in Vrgin Most was the mayor, Obradovic, and the chief of police, Djuro Skaljac. So the Republic of Serbian Krajina was an alien introduction into the picture. I did not require or expect to deal with unison Republic of Serbian Krajina in anything. If I wanted to make a discussion or discuss the issue of deployment in Vrgin Most, I go to the mayor and the chief of police. That's how I thought we would operate at the beginning or go to Vojnic, which is another municipality, or any other municipality. Now in this paragraph I'm told they raise a Republic of Serbian Krajina, it's a government, and its headquarters in Knin. That's a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- did you -- in your dealings, because you clearly were put in the position of having dealings with them, did you in any sense refuse to recognise the RSK officials in any formal sense?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, let me put it this way: I wouldn't say refused. They were our clients. These are our counterparts in dealing with them. Without offending them, I went out of my way to deal with them the only way I was instructed to deal with them. If they insisted their Republic of Krajina at certain point, as you can see the language filtered here, it was a de facto. So if it was a de facto situation, without offending anyone, we would deal with them that way, but we wouldn't be in a rush to accord them that designation, that of statehood that they sought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first came across Mr. Slobodan Lazarevic on -- it was pretty much immediately on your arrival in Sector North in April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. He had been, by his own telling me, he was switching from having worked for the EMM to us. EMM, the European Monitoring Mission, had already been deployed there before we arrived. According to him, he was working with them first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd said -- the reference is paragraph 21 of your statement -- you described him at that time as being a liaison officer for the local Serb authorities with the UN. Now, first at that time you didn't know of the existence of RSK or of the -- well, government, without any admission on your part, that government in Knin?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, but almost a few weeks -- when I met him, he was not even liaison for RSK. He worked himself into liaison of RSK within weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he continue to be, to some extent, also liaison for other local Serb officials from the -- well, if I say opstinas, my case manager is deeply offended by the pluralisation of opstina but I'm going to use it, we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked himself from a civilian interpreter and somebody with normal flashy clothes to full camouflage uniform by the middle of June, and he was the right-hand man of the commander Cedo Bulat for Kordun, and that meant he had at least almost undisputed influence or authority in Kordun, which made up all those opstinas that your colleague might be whispering in your ears, from Vrgin Most to Vojnic to Slunj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you refer, and this is paragraph 48 of your statement, you refer to Mr. Lazarevic, as you do frequently, and talk about what you've just talked about, his graduation to camouflage uniform. You say that he would frequently make incendiary radio broadcasts -- this is paragraph 48, did I say that? - apparently to the delight of his mentors. So who were his mentors in that context?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all I was always the recipient of which side was taking offence to what. The characterisation of incendiary was from the Croat side which was monitoring the radio broadcast from Petrova Gora, direction Zagreb. And if you stand on Petrova Gora you can see the entire city of Zagreb. So Mr. Lazarevic would get on the radio about 4.00, 5.00 and make some broadcast about the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was a read matter, and that broadcast would be received in Zagreb, and lo and behold, I'm on the carpet on the other side, "What are these local Serbs doing," and they're making this incendiary broadcast. Delight -- he actually went into that radio -- I went into that radio tower when he was doing it, and you can see all the mirth and all the delight when they were talking about whatever they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say Mr. Lazarevic methodically developed a close relationship with Colonel Bulat, the commander of RSK forces in the Kordun region. What was the extent of your contacts and dealings with Colonel Bulat?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extensive. The first few months of our presence there when my colleagues, like the report you have seen here from civil affairs and others, are helping me on the civil UN police side, I was always in the meetings with this general who commanded the sector with each of the parties that were required in order to demobilise along the confrontation line and inside the sector. So I met -- in order to demobilise Kordun area, we had numerous meetings with Colonel Bulat at his own headquarters. But that is the military headquarters. There were brigade commands all around. So meeting with him became almost routine, two or three times a week in the first few months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you describe - this is paragraph 49 of your statement - you describe efforts of the RSK officials with Lazarevic acting as a facilitator to corrupt or compromise the first sector commander. My first question is: Was Colonel Bulat one of the people who was associated with that -- those attempts to corrupt or compromise the first sector commander?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we met, and we met in different places, in different houses, their own houses, Colonel Bulat is soldier. Like most soldiers, when they are talking to each other, they are mostly economic with their words. There is not too much said, and there is very little bravado around. So he left all the talking, when you're talking extraordinary and everything, to Lazarevic. So most of the work, if you thought -- if you like, most of the elaboration and all of that, he left that to his friend Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think an army lawyer would fit into that description that you've just given. Your reference to attempt to corrupt or compromise the first sector commander, that was Brigadier General Bamaiyi; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by -- well, I assume that they were attempts in they were not successful. That's -- you'd confirm that, would you, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they? How -- how were they attempting to corrupt or compromise Brigadier General Bamaiyi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazarevic went out of his way to make the general comfortable, make -- be helpful, be on call of duty. But the general, knowing his job like any other, he would come down like 16 tonnes about what he wants. So he would come over there, and he used to call him in his booming voice, Lazarevic, where is the demobilisation that I wanted like yesterday? So in order to stall, in order to stall his attempt to get what he wanted done, that's what I'm referring to. He would usually scuttle things or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attempt to scuttle things, to stall. He didn't succeed. The sector was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can we move on to paragraph 64 of your statement, please. Now, I think everybody would acknowledge this is a fairly key item in the evidence you've been giving. This is your meeting on the 26th of May, 1992, with Mr. Borojevic, the mayor of Dvor, and the chief -- the police chief in Dvor, and so on. And, first of all, you were being informed, weren't you, and now, you found this strange, didn't you, that you were being informed by the mayor of Dvor that the mayor of Bosanski Novi was requesting passage through Krajina for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the starting point is that the mayor of Dvor was from a place which was within your sector, your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mayor of Bosanski Novi wasn't.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on that particular point, why was it so strange that that request would be passed on to you through an official who was from within the -- your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, we were there for a different agenda, which he knew. His agenda had to do with the UN presence in his Dvor area. He sets all that aside, and he's talking about across the border where we had no presence, and kind of not even what you would call an aside on parenthesis. No. That became the main agenda. It told me that there is more than casual interest like I got a request by a colleague mayor and I'm just passing to you, something you would do in a meeting parenthetically. "I got this request, you can talk to the meeting if you have the time. Now can we get on with the agenda?" No. It was the agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the mayor of Bosanski Novi, of course, is Mr. Pasic. At this point, had you -- I'm afraid if it's there in black and white then I simply forget it, but at this point had you ever met Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you -- you declined what was suggested to you because you expressed, as you've described in your evidence, this goes on into paragraph 67 of your statement, you -- it seems that you made very clear your view of how unsatisfactory this approach was and how unsatisfactory it was that this request should be being channeled through the mayor of Dvor. That's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Counsellor. What I made clear was not the dissatisfaction, not even the channel. What I made clear was it doesn't sound believable. At that point I knew nothing, I'm there for something else. And he's telling me this, and when I query him, he wouldn't have all the ready answers, and he sensed I'm not believing what he is saying. And as I recount the story at that stage, sensing that disbelief, he walks across from where we were meeting in a conference room, which was next to his own office, picks up the phone and dials mayor or what he called Mayor Pasic and says would you like, if you don't believe me, talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your -- one of your unhappinesses about all this at that time was that it was -- you were being told something which you regarded as third-hand, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were being told by the mayor of Dvor what the mayor of Bosanski Novi was saying the Muslim were saying?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were saying. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were given the opportunity then of at least speaking with the mayor of Bosanski Novi, so you -- to reduce, if you like, third-hand to secondhand; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't take that opportunity to at least cut it down from third-hand to secondhand.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't think I -- I was ready to take it at that time. Besides, as I believe, to the point of Your Honour telling the other learned counsel that he understood the internal workings of the UN, I had to -- I had these constraints that tells me your area of responsibility is this one. Don't get out. So that was also weighed in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say -- this is paragraph 68 of your statement. You say that after that meeting -- well, you say at the end of paragraph 67 that you never called Pasic but you met soon thereafter. And then in paragraph 68, you say: "After this meeting I concluded that mayors of Dvor and Bosanski Novi were acting in concert." Just goes up -- you're talking about after the meeting on the 26th of May. You're not talking about after having met Pasic, are you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I concluded that the mayor of Dvor has more than a casual interest in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- excuse me one moment, Your Honour. I'll just get the piece of paper. You -- so after your meeting with the mayor of Dvor and the others who accompanied him but not including Mr. Pasic, you say you concluded - this is paragraph 68 - that those two mayors were acting in concert to engineer a massive evacuation under the guise of humanitarian assistance beginning with some 5.000 Muslim residents. Your report of this meeting appears, or your note following this meeting is Exhibit P125. I think you'll probably need to be handed that again, Mr. Kirudja. Now, I don't want to read the whole thing into the record again. I'm quite sure it's already there. But if you just want to please refresh your mind. It's your writing, but if you could just read the first page and then I want to go over to the second page. It's all -- this is your note of 26 May 1992. I'm sure that the contents are already read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I think you're invited to read it for yourself, the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do it quietly. I am reading it but, Your Honour, I'm guided by you; is it loudly or quietly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, just if the witness would read it to himself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just picking up the last three lines on that first page then, "Would appreciate if UNHCR could assist in obtaining accurate and first-hand information," because you referred to the third-hand nature of the information. "... first-hand information on the story, UNPROFOR would also be grateful for advice and cooperation with UNHCR on handling the issue. We have indications that this story may have other political ramifications." Now, I'm just contrasting that with the conclusion that you express in paragraph 68 of your statement where you say conclusion that they were engineering a massive evacuation under the guise of humanitarian assistance. You appear to have downplayed that rather in your written report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason for downplaying it was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Internal. Internal. This is the first time -- I got the clear details from Mayor Borojevic, not just about the 5.000 but the demand that we film it, and guarantee -- I got the whole works from him. Notice none of that is here. I just distilled it to 5.000 Muslims who have been promised by Serbs that they could be guaranteed a safe passage through the UNPA to destinations in Germany and Austria. Headquarters internally don't take fast-breaking news massively. You tend to send them distilled and build on it because headquarters -- I mean UN. You want them to get the gist first. The second element: At this moment I was still working on having a proper staffing inclusive of an UNHCR representative with me in the office. So this was designed, therefore, to achieve that, as also the basis for which I wanted to expedite the presence of deployment of UNHCR person into the centre. So it's not downplaying it, it's distilling it to the essence that I wanted to be paid attention up the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about UN headquarters, are you talking about your headquarters in Zagreb for your purposes or are you talking --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. You're not talking back to New York or anywhere, Geneva or anywhere like that. The -- at paragraph 74 of your statement, you're having a meeting with Mr. Pasic. I think it's on the 27th of May if we look back in your statement. So we take it that it was the 27th of May. And you've got a Serb delegation, including Mr. Pasic. So you've got somebody, of course, from Bosnia-Herzegovina there, and you asked what had changed in Bosanski Novi. Why couldn't Serbs and Muslims live together, and so on. And then Mr. Pasic replies to you -- well, I'm sorry, I should perhaps read the whole thing. "The former police officers" -- "Pasic replied the former police officers who were Muslims refused to sign loyalty oaths to the new government. I asked when this new government had been formed and when oaths of loyalty to this new government became a requirement. And Mr. Pasic replied, I cannot say when the new Serbian government was formed but it was before the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And you say, "I understood this to mean that the mayor did not know the exact date of the formation of the new Serbian Republic of BiH." Is it -- I'm not quite clear here, Mr. Kirudja, but is it that the existence of this new government was news to you at this point at that -- at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. This was news to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- although you maybe don't remember the exact date, Mr. Kirudja, I take it that at some point you came to know that the -- just a slightly different name as you give it there, Serbian Republic of BiH, in it's own language, of course, actually it was established on the 9th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, Counsellor. And you might also want to connect that with an earlier testimony in the earlier pages. There was talk of new reality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the first person to bring that to our attention was General Spiro Nikovic when he was telling us why -- what will replace what he was leaving behind. And when I asked what's going on, he said, "We have a --" used a language close to what Mayor Pasic used, "new reality." But he proceeded to name -- said the former Yugoslavia would be replaced by six countries, and proceeded to name them. There is a paragraph in the testimony --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- naming them. If you look at that paragraph, he did not deconstruct BH. He left it. He named it BiH. He was not deconstructing it. He added a new element to the six countries; you can see on the list there is RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 28 is the paragraph in your statement.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't work from memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're accurately reflecting what's in your own paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. When this mayor now came to talk to us and said "new reality," I had that in mind, so I'm trying to ask him what is the new reality, and that's when he introduced the deconstruction of BiH by naming Serbian Republic of BiH, and in that sense it was news to me at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- of course the recognition -- the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as we said earlier, was 6th of April, 1992. So the formation before the international recognition was actually three months before, but you -- you had not heard of Republika Srpska as an entity at this point.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether, talking about at this point, I wonder whether that would be a suitable point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this time that would be a suitable point. Yes. We will adjourn until ten minutes to one, but I have one very specific question to you, Mr. Stewart: Does the Defence intend to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do have -- we do have one, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a single sheet, actually. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If possible, could you provide that to the registrar already during the break, not necessarily with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. I hadn't -- in fact, earlier I hadn't expect to get to it today, but I think I may now, so we will do that during this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn until ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, could we go on and look at paragraph 81 of your statement, please. That's at page 21. You say: "During these kinds of meetings," and you just talked about a meeting with sector commander and others and so on, "meetings with Croatian and Serbian military representatives, both sides often claimed that terrorists were infiltrating across the confrontation line. We heard this claim repeatedly from the Serb side." In fact, did you hear the claim from both sides?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both sides met on the Bosnian international border where the Muslims -- Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. You say that in the first sentence. But you're saying you heard it repeatedly from the Serb side, but is it right to say that you actually heard it pretty frequently from the Croatian side as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not frequently, but now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then eventually -- you go on to say: "Eventually it became evident that, true or not, they advanced this claim mostly to justify their continued refusal to disarm totally as required by the Vance Plan." Now, you're not suggesting that claims of infiltration were not, in fact, in many instances true on both sides, are you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm allowing for certain incidents to be seen in context. There were times when we were told infiltrators are -- have come through the border, and for days or weeks thereafter we would see no evidence. But there were occasions where there were people arrested as a result of having crossed the border. A massive incident occurred in August, or September, August, where within two, three days there were 600 Muslims in the prison at Glina having attempted to cross from Bihac pocket into -- into Slunj side of that. So there were times when we had evidence, and there were times that we were told there are terrorists, and we do our best to find the evidence, and that's why I'm saying true or not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you could be given Exhibit P133, which is your own memorandum of the 16th of June. So that was actually about 11 days after the particular meeting you're referring to in paragraph 80. I want to make it clear, Mr. Kirudja, I'm not going to be exploring with you some sort of ghoulish balance sheet with who did what matched against who did what. That's not what I'm engaged on, but if we look at paragraph 1 of your memorandum attached to the front sheet, 16th of June, 1992, you are writing: "The humanitarian situation in Bihac is rapidly deteriorating. The meeting held on 1 June 1992 in Bihac at the request of the military -- UN military observers and the mayor of Bihac was an attempt to alert the international community to a humanitarian disaster in the making. Armed elements in the area terrorised the population on both sides of the border. A stream of vindictive killings, forced mass movement of persons, and other horrible reprisals have been reported to UNPROFOR." So it's not -- you're not giving numbers and all that sort of thing, but that's -- that was an accurate reflection of the position in mid-June 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we go on then, please, to paragraph 87 of your statement. On the 16th of June, and that is actually exactly the document we've just been looking at. "On the 16th of June, I reported to our Zagreb headquarters," and you wanted to highlight as clearly as you could the urgent need for humanitarian operation, and so on, and that's that document. And you said: "In my opinion, Serb stories of atrocities committed by Muslims, such as axing to death 40 Serbs in a two-day period, were part of a concerted effort by Serbian leaders on both sides of the border to paint their Muslims in the area as dangerous." Mr. Kirudja, a story such as the axing to death of 40 Serbs in a two-day period, it could have been true, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly my earlier comment. When we were told that, we'd do our best to try to gather evidence. In this particular case, we were, despite our pleas, to say once you get an information that 40 people have been axed to death within where you have been deployed, never mind whether they are Serbs or Muslims, we want to know and get at it. So we didn't get to that. But it isn't a complaint I'm making, it's an observation I'm making that there was a tendency to flash the atrocities on the Serb side and a failure to follow up with us and bring us face-to-face with the reality. That was repeated more often. On the paragraph you read, when we're -- where non-Serbs are involved, we are brought face-to-face with that reality not on the Serb side but on the receiving side, the side that receives that kind of treatment. They bring that to our attention in an attempt to get either protection or redress. Those 40 Serbs that you're referring to, Counsellor, I'm not sure that you looked at the document that I referred to at the bottom of that document to be sure that there were not a number of 40 Serbs. I heard repeatedly in the area of Dvor on that side of the border where the Serbs controlled both sides. That's the difficulties I'm referring to. They would tell me something happened, "But we took care of it," they would tell me. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we go on to -- it's convenient to do it by reference to your statement at paragraph 98 of your statement. It's actually a citation from your -- or quotation from your report, which is P139, but it's more convenient simply to use the statement. It's the report in which you say: "We believe the football field detainees are only the tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina trying to establish a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina free of Muslims. In that process, the mayors, the milicija, and the TDF of Bosanski Novi were acting in unison with their counterparts," and so on. Is it correct, Mr. Kirudja that you at that time had no knowledge whatever of any involvement or direction of any of these events from Sarajevo or Pale by SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I had no direct connection between Pale and these events coming to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say Sarajevo or Pale, just to make it clear, the -- the SDS leadership moved from Sarajevo to Pale in early April. I think it was the 10th of April, 1992. I don't know whether you're aware of that now.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on. That's why my answer to you earlier was in reference to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- in your evidence yesterday afternoon, you were asked by His Honour Judge Orie -- not yesterday afternoon. I hope you were enjoying the holiday yesterday, Mr. Kirudja. On Friday afternoon, you were asked about Exhibit P140. I wonder if you might be given that. A report from Mr. Paolo Raffone, of whom we've heard quite a number of times in evidence, released by you. And the particular point was the penultimate paragraph of the report or the memorandum, where he says that the president of the Executive Council and deputy president of the Crisis Committee in Dubica, that's Bosanska Dubica, announced a recent decision of the Crisis Committee approved by the parliament of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or it would be Republika Srpska by this time, regarding the necessity to disband the structure of the SDA and put all its members under control. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The first question is: Do you have any personal knowledge of this item at all or is the limit of what you know simply what Mr. Raffone is reporting to you here?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter. The limit is what Mr. Raffone is reporting. Counsellor, with the understanding that when he's at that meeting, he's just listening to a speaker through interpretation and taking note of what he heard, and that's it. What he heard from the speaker and reporting what he heard directly from these representatives which he has named in the memo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any procedures which existed in the parliament -- in Republika Srpska Assembly or parliament, as we might call it, at that time for approval or endorsement or ratification of such decisions of Crisis Committees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any such approval ever having been sought by any local organ in -- within Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you, please, just one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is the one I mentioned immediately before the break. We provided copies to Ms. Philpott just before the break, Your Honour. May I explain that it's a single sheet of paper. It's in Serbian, or B/C/S as it's called. We have an informal translation but we haven't, in the time available to us, we haven't been able to have it translated. It's been or is being submitted to the translation. Yes. It -- Ms. Cmeric will submit it to the Translation Unit immediately at the close of business today. Your Honour, what I was suggesting -- was proposing to the Trial Chamber is it's a single sheet of paper, it's not a long document. I think when I wasn't here in court last week on one occasion the procedure was adopted that Ms. Cmeric, who reads Serbian considerably better than I do, to say the least, that perhaps if Ms. Cmeric were to read it and then it would be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Interpreters have a copy of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They have the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have the original in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially if Ms. Ceric would read slowly, and then we could read the English and see whether there are any divergencies between what we hear and what we read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is there an exhibit number on this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we only get the number for the first one since the translation is not yet official, and that would be Defence --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit number D15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we, Mr. Harmon, if you also could read carefully when we hear the translation and then afterwards we could see whether the unofficial translation would do for the purposes we have here and -- I mean, if there's hardly any difference, then of course, we could try to give it D15, that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm quite happy to give Mr. Harmon my translation right now for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon did not receive the translation. Oh, yes. Well, if -- if we would even put it on the ELMO so we could all read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The translation goes on to two pages but the original is one page. I'm sorry, I didn't turn on the microphone, Your Honour. The translation goes on to two pages but the original document is a single page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just see whether it becomes any -- yes. And, Mr. Usher, could you please keep a close eye on the reading so if you would follow it in English that you immediately move from page 1 to page 2 once we're there. Ms. Cmeric, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Novi. Number: 01/1- and then in handwriting, 023-120/92. Date: 18 June 1992. The text of the document is as follows: "Pursuant to Article 186, paragraph 52 of the municipal statute of Bosanski Novi ('Official Gazette of the municipality of Bosanski Novi', number 21/90), the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Novi at its Assembly held on the 16th of June, 1992, has adopted the following conclusion: "I. 1. The report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi is hereby adopted, and the conclusions, orders, and other decisions it reached are hereby confirmed. "2. With respect to the Muslim population on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, the positions of the Municipal Board of the SDS are hereby adopted: "- that citizens of Muslim nationalities may move out from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi voluntarily in an organised and civilised manner. "- to strictly prohibit any activities that might be directed at forcible relocation of the population. "- that persons in the collection centre of the Mlakve stadium should be treated humanely and in compliance with the regulations referring to persons deprived of their liberty and prisoners. "3. The municipal Territorial Defence Staff is required to urgently undertake all necessary measures and activities to establish a brigade of the battalion type - of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "4. The public security station of Bosanski Novi and the command of the military police are hereby ordered to on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi establish public law and order and security for citizens. "II. These conclusions shall be published in 'The Official Gazette of the municipality Bosanski Novi.' President of the Municipal Assembly Radomir Pasic, signed and stamped."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where there are changes, I would say to the extent of any significance at all, it's the word "accepted" is translated by our translators -- by "adopted" rather than by "accepted," "verified" is translated as "confirmed," and the reception centre in the provisional translation became a collection centre, and in the first bullet under 2, it reads in the unofficial translation that the citizens of the Muslim nationality can move out, where it was translated by our interpreters as may move out. Apart from smaller and less significant divergences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think the only -- the only fairly -- I wouldn't say trivial, tiny rather than trivial, is that it's "humanely" rather than "humanly" but that's obvious, but otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps there are two issues, rather, of reading, and that is first of all the first line it says it's 011/ and then I'm not quite sure what is 023 could under no circumstances be 823, but I'm not familiar with how handwriting is taught at school. And then the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's locally different. And the second issue is the date here is translated as the 16th of June, and Judge El Mahdi has at least some doubts as to whether it's really 16 or whether the second number would be anything else than a 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It looks like an 8 to me, Your Honour. If Judge El Mahdi is thinking it could be an 8, then I would, with respect, share his view that it could easily be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's really a matter of reading than of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know what the best copy we've got is but, Your Honour, it would seem more likely that the 023 is 023 because it looks as if it's going number 23 to 120. So it would start as a 023 rather than as an 823, but we can, so far as it matters, Your Honour, no doubt check that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on at this moment and let's try to get an official and final translation, but we can work on the basis of this provisional translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd only like to say, Your Honour, that it looked like a pretty good unofficial translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who made it, but it deserves full --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do; Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to give already the -- express the appreciation without even knowing that it was Ms. Cmeric who deserves it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja -- after that, we may not take very long, it depends. Mr. Kirudja, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection or knowledge of this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It only reminds me in content, only part of it, to a document we looked at on Friday, the one from the same Radomir Pasic addressed to civil affairs coordinator in Sector North. Could I ask kindly that document -- I also want to know the date of that document, the one that was shown on Friday. It is stamped and signed by him as president of Crisis Committee, and it is addressed to me -- to the headquarters sector, and it is partly translated in English, and you are shown both a badly translated copy and a Serbian copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have that copy. I can assist the Chamber and the witness. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 141. The date appears on that document to be 6 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6 July 1992. And as I listened to your exchange, the one you have just read in translation is either the 18th or the 16th, whichever date you settle with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of June.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents in those two documents strike me as interesting in the sense that they have some similarities and some significant departures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you -- well, do you wish to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to comment on that departure and similarity, because it strikes me as important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can have both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I might have back from somebody the unofficial English translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- of the document that we looked at just now, the new one. Or if it can be brought up on the ELMO. I don't mind which, but I need one or the other, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like similarities first, Mr. Kirudja, or which?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The similarity I note is on paragraph 2 of the translation, bullet number 1, that citizens of the Muslim nationality can move out of the Bosanski Novi municipality voluntarily, in an organised and civilised manner. The similarity with the previous document dated July 6th, it's a month later, is that issue of voluntarily, to move voluntarily. It's in the paragraph that reads: "People -- permit -- permit for voluntary abandon of municipality territory in direction of inhabited places in the Republic of Croatia." That striked me as somewhat similar in terms of the claim that such a movement was voluntary. In an organised and civilised manner is a difference, because in this letter of July, he is precisely asking for an organisation of the movement. In June, in your translation, the movement hadn't happened, obviously. It says that it was going to happen. It was going to be organised and civilised. That is a slight difference. Thirdly, in this memo of July 6th, P141.1, there is that paragraph that talks about - and I'm reading the badly translated paragraph - "Status of immovable property is salved --" I think it is sold but it is written there "salved," "-- on the basis of exchange with citizens of Serbian nationality, refugees to Bosanski Novi municipality from Republic of Croatia and Republic of Slovenia for their property left in mentioned countries less number of citizens of Muslims and other nationalities sailed or gave --" meaning sold, I translate that -- "or give like gift their property about what they have all official documentation. Citizens of Muslim and other nationalities are taking their movable property with them after making of official specification." Can you move this ELMO a little up, please, for this, a little bit. This item 2 of the document that you read dated 18th has the sentence that: "Any activities that would aim at forcible moving out of population be strictly forbidden." That's a significant difference. There is no reference a month later to prohibition of forcible moving of anyone. Third, that individuals at the reception centre of Mlakve stadium shall be treated humanely. I assume that is the understanding of that translation, and in accordance with the regulation relating to individuals deprived of freedom and prisoners. None of these two elements appear a month later in the letter given to us. On the contrary. The emphasis on sale, exchange of property and all of that is reiterated. So those are the similarities and differences that I see. And I also mentioned on Friday that this letter of July 6th follows our letter to Mr. Pasic dated 20th of June. 20th of June. That is personally telling him what he is planning to do is unacceptable to us. That was on 20th of June. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I just now would like to refer you to something else, which is that you -- excuse me one moment, Your Honour. You gave evidence previously -- well, I think you've given evidence in two previous cases before this Tribunal. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case and the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the Brdjanin case -- what I wish to do, and Your Honour, I hope this will be convenient, there's a passage of about four pages of Mr. Kirudja's evidence in the Brdjanin case. What I would propose to do, with Your Honour's permission, is read as quickly as is consistent with helping the interpreters do their job --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Mr. Stewart, I take it that we'll not finish today, certainly not after you have to read four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will. We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because otherwise I would have invited you to give us the four pages. But if you say by reading it, even if we have got no copies, slowly, we will finish within 30 minutes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. It's actually because I'm going to finish today that I haven't got the copies, because I'd expected to get to this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll get the right glasses back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence-in-chief, it was, in the Brdjanin case -- and the page reference for everybody who has these in their pockets is 14545 in the Brdjanin case. It was Wednesday, the 12th of February, 2003, and you were being examined by Ms. Korner, and she says at -- she's asking a question: "As we have stated --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have neither the monitor nor the document he is talking about. The monitor is blank, and I don't have the document he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are no copies of the document, but I think we have to push the transcript button and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to just make a few notes and have certain passages repeated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We also have monitors where we can scroll back, so we could then it repeat it, because once it left your screen, it's gone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that I have a monitor, it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The monitor is going to give you the transcript today so that you can check back. The case reference, which may be required by somebody, I don't know, is IT-99-36-T, because it was in trial, the Brdjanin case. Ms. Korner referred you to paragraph 11 of some document or other: "As we have stated in the preceding sitreps a nominal international border divides the Serb controlled opstinas of Dvor and Kostajnica in Krajina from the Serb controlled opstinas of Novi and Dubica across the River Una." I think this is a document we have seen in this case as well anyway, so it's all -- should be fairly familiar territory for you. "Beyond these two or three other opstinas, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Banja Luka in Northern Bosnia, which fall under the so-called Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, the two Serbian republics economically depend on a corridor linking them with Serbia and Montenegro. There is also a growing evidence of a common military strategy or alliance in this regard, and observing the military structure on the ground, there are signs that Banja Luka may be exercising a balance of military power over Knin in a way analogous to the power exercised by Belgrade prior to the proclamation of a new federal Yugoslavia. The present supreme military commander in Knin is --" And then Judge Agius interjected: "Reportedly." Ms. Korner continued: "Reportedly from Banja Luka while the previous one is said to be shuttling between the two capitals. Further, we have noticed the tendency of certain local authorities here to periodically retreat to Banja Luka or Belgrade at critical times. Now, can we deal -- split that. The military signs that there was control being exercised or -- I'm sorry, the balance of military power from Banja Luka, where were you getting that information from?" So that was Ms. Korner's question. And your answer was: "This sentence following that actually contains the answer to your question. We were tracing who was commanding, where they were going and that, basically." Ms. Korner, question: "All right. Now as to the tendency of certain local authorities here to periodically retreat to Banja Luka or Belgrade at critical times, in your dealings with the political authorities, the local ones, did you get any impression that they were -- as to what their powers were to take decisions?" Your answer: "I can speak directly with regard to the sector because I was in daily arm's-length relationship with them. Every opstina that was part of that sector had two interweaved power structure; the military side and the civil side. The military side we have spoken at length.
