On the civil side, there were mayors, the so-called mayors of opstina A, B, or C who also had the police, the chief of police, the opstina A, B, or C. This group had the least influence in a way. They were, on the other hand, the most heard about political issues, like we won't live together with the Serbs with the other non-Serbs. They were the most expressive when it comes to what was going on, even militarily, explaining it out. The military side normally didn't give -- were not given to giving speeches. So much of the political drive, most of the explanation was coming from the civil side of the structure. Most of the action, on the other hand, was taking place on the military side." Question from Ms. Korner. "You say they had a tendency to retreat to Banja Luka. To do what? Or Belgrade." Your answer: "You have to think of -- again I was speaking about mayors and other people located in the sector. They were surrounded on the confrontation line by the Croats, in the direction of Karlovac, Sisak and Zagreb. Another way of putting it, too, they were also blockaded themselves. They didn't mention that, the Serbs, were blockaded in that sense. Economically they can't go out and they couldn't get their fuel, for example. They couldn't get most normal things, because of the war, the electricity was not working, because things had been broken up -- broken down, and without the political -- the grid, electrical grid, normal things weren't working, like water, because they were all pumped. So in a way, there was a situation of shortages even for the Serbs. So for them to redress that, they had to get out somehow, and that's the corridor that took them to Banja Luka or Belgrade for the purposes of redressing shortages in normal, everyday economic life." Question: "In dealing with the mayors of these local areas such as Novi, Kostajnica or Dvor, did they ever say to you or did you ever get the impression that they had to take instructions from their superiors?" Answer: "The fact that they all seemed to replicate each other in the same language was a very good indication that if you think of it like a choir, they were all singing from a sheet that was passed around." Question: "Right. Sorry, can you just --" Answer: "And there was very little situations where they would deviate from that, from that -- whatever was politically correct, and we can go into details of that. You could hardly find anybody who would deviate from that." Question: "Right. And that led you to believe what? I'm sorry to ask you this." That must have meant "I'm sorry to have to ask you this, but we need to have it stated clearly for the terms of the transcript." Answer: "If there were the Serbs inside the sector, that script, that choreography pointed at Knin as a centre of coordination of authority." "Right." "Right" was the question, in effect, from Ms. Korner. Answer from you: "If you are in the Bihac areas we mentioned, outside the Bihac pocket, then I mentioned point us to Banja Luka but mostly Belgrade." "Thank you. All right." And then -- well, I'll stop there. Mr. Kirudja, is there anything in that evidence which you gave to the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case that you would not be entirely content to have constitute part of your evidence in this case before this Tribunal in that whole passage that I read out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, I will answer that question in two parts. With respect to fact, I am quite comfortable with what is said in that. The accuracy of what I said I will stand by. On the second part, whether it is useful in this trial, Your Honour, I leave it to you as lawyers and Judges what is useful in one trial or the other, not being a lawyer, I would consider that something outside my ability to respond to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think the Trial Chamber would probably, with respect, endorse that view, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Kirudja. Thank you very much, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on whether we'll ask you to come back tomorrow, Mr. Kirudja, but if we would do so, it would be only for a very short time. I'd like to know whether there's any need for re-examination, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's indulgence, I would like to review the testimony he has given and just consider it this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Specifically, I'd like to refer to the transcripts that have been referred to that I don't have at my disposal in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'd rather use the next break, although a very long one, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I hope that you have not made any travel arrangements yet for this afternoon and that you could still be with us tomorrow morning, although presumably not for a very long time. The Judges might have some questions for you, counsel for the Prosecution might have some questions for you. Perhaps if there's any need to ask further questions by the Defence on the basis of any questions put to you by the Bench or by the Prosecution. But there's hardly any doubt in my mind, to just to use my words as cautious as you seem to use your words, that it will not -- that tomorrow, perhaps after one, not more than one and a half hours, you would be excused. So if you want to make any travel arrangements or if they have to be made for you, I think we could safely say that tomorrow in the afternoon you will certainly be able to freely move wherever you'd like to go. May I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony given in this court and still to be given. We will then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in Courtroom I, a different courtroom from than this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
